screens.title: External Functions and Stored Procedures
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will explore two complementary extension points in Snowflake: External Functions and Stored Procedures. External Functions let your S Q L queries call out to existing serverless services, enabling row-level enrichment, validation, or specialized compute that lives outside Snowflake. Stored Procedures let you encapsulate multi-step logic, DDL and DML, and control flow inside Snowflake using S Q L scripting or JavaScript. You'll learn the architecture for an External Function — how an A P I Integration and an A P I Gateway route a request to a serverless function — and the key S Q L commands used to register that integration and the function itself. I will point out common mistakes, like misconfigured allowed prefixes or concatenating unvalidated input into S Q L strings, and practical trade-offs, such as network latency for external calls versus the power of in-platform execution. By the end you'll know when to choose an External Function and when a Stored Procedure is the right tool, and you'll have concrete examples to try in a live coding demo.

screens.title: External Functions: Architecture & Use Cases
screens.narratorSegment: External Functions let Snowflake queries call code that runs outside the platform. The architecture centers on three pieces: an A P I Integration object in Snowflake, an A P I Gateway that acts as a front door, and a serverless function that executes your logic. The A P I Integration stores the trust relationship and allowed endpoint prefixes; the gateway routes the request to the serverless function; and Snowflake serializes inputs and deserializes outputs for S Q L consumption. A typical use case is enriching rows with third-party data — for example, calling a sentiment model for each row of text. This is powerful because it avoids extract-transform-load cycles, but it introduces network latency, so it is best for cases where the external logic is complex and cannot be efficiently implemented in S Q L. Common misconfigurations include incorrect allowed prefixes and role ARNs, which lead to authorization failures. As a concrete example, imagine calling a sentiment endpoint for each product review during a reporting query; use sampling in testing and measure latency. A misconception to avoid is thinking External Functions are free of operational cost: they rely on your cloud functions and gateway, so plan for retries, throttling, and error handling. Takeaway: use External Functions when external compute is essential and row-level enrichment value outweighs network cost. How would you measure whether the network cost is acceptable for your query pattern?

content.html:
Core Concept
External Function Architecture
Snowflake → API Integration → API Gateway → Serverless Function. Each piece enforces security and routing.
API Integration secures Snowflake's access and lists allowed prefixes.
API Gateway routes requests to your function and enforces network access.
Serverless executes custom logic and returns serialized results.
Key Takeaway

Use External Functions for specialized external compute, and measure latency and error handling before broad adoption.

Architecture Diagram (annotated cards)
Snowflake
Calls External Function as a UDF inside SQL
API Integration
Defines role ARNs and allowed prefixes
API Gateway
Fronts your serverless function
Serverless Function
Performs enrichment or specialized compute
Concrete example
Example: Call a sentiment endpoint for each review row to append a sentiment label during a reporting query. Use sampling to measure latency and error rates before running at scale.
Common mistake: mismatched API_ALLOWED_PREFIXES or wrong IAM role ARN causes authorization errors. Check these values first when troubleshooting.

screens.title: Create an API Integration
screens.narratorSegment: Creating an A P I Integration is the first concrete step to enable External Functions. This process establishes a trust relationship and records which endpoints Snowflake may call. The S Q L pattern starts with CREATE OR REPLACE A P I INTEGRATION, followed by provider-specific parameters and API_ALLOWED_PREFIXES that list the gateway URL prefixes. For AWS A P I Gateway you provide an IAM role ARN which Snowflake will assume; for other providers similar values are required. A common error is forgetting to include the full URL prefix in API_ALLOWED_PREFIXES; this will cause authorization failures when the External Function is invoked. As an example, imagine you have an A P I Gateway URL that ends with a path to your function. Include the prefix up to the function base path in API_ALLOWED_PREFIXES. Always test the integration with a minimal external function call and check the error messages — they usually indicate whether the failure is due to the role ARN or allowed prefixes. Misconception: the A P I Integration does not deploy your function; it only authorizes Snowflake to call a gateway. After the integration, you still need to define the External Function that references the gateway endpoint. Try a dry run with one test row to validate the configuration before bulk use.

keyIdea.title: Integration checklist
keyIdea.text: Set provider, role ARN, enable flag, and allowed prefixes correctly; test with a single call to verify authorization.

content.html:
Process Flow
Create API INTEGRATION
Follow this SQL pattern and validate the placeholders and prefixes carefully.
-- As ACCOUNTADMIN or a role with CREATE INTEGRATION privilege
CREATE OR REPLACE API INTEGRATION my_api_integration
  API_PROVIDER = AWS_API_GATEWAY
  API_AWS_ROLE_ARN = 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/my-api-gateway-role'
  ENABLED = TRUE
  API_ALLOWED_PREFIXES = ('https://abcdef123.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/prod/my_function');
1. API_PROVIDER selects your gateway provider.
2. API_AWS_ROLE_ARN grants Snowflake permission to assume a role.
3. API_ALLOWED_PREFIXES lists exact gateway URL prefixes to authorize.
Common Mistake

Using an incomplete allowed prefix or incorrect ARN is the most frequent cause of integration failures. Verify exact gateway URL and role ARN early in testing.

Quick verification steps
  1. Confirm the IAM role has permission to invoke the gateway or be assumed by Snowflake.
  2. Ensure the gateway stage and path match the allowed prefix exactly.
  3. Run a controlled External Function call with a single test row and inspect errors.
Analogy
Think of API Integration as a permission slip: it doesn't open the door, but it tells Snowflake where it's allowed to knock.
Key Takeaway

Create the integration with exact prefixes and test a single call. Integration enables authorization, it doesn’t deploy or run the serverless code.

screens.title: Define and Call an External Function
screens.narratorSegment: Once the A P I Integration is in place, define an External Function that references the gateway endpoint. The CREATE OR REPLACE EXTERNAL FUNCTION statement maps a function name and parameter signature to a URL. Snowflake treats the function like any other UDF in S Q L, so you can SELECT it or use it in transformations. The important security detail is that the function uses API_INTEGRATION to assert the trust established earlier, and the endpoint must match the allowed prefix. An example call looks like SELECT my_external_sentiment_analyzer('This product is great!'); which returns a VARCHAR result from the external service. A misconception to clear up: defining the External Function does not automatically make the external service secure; you must ensure the gateway and function enforce appropriate authorization and input validation. Also, external calls introduce per-row network latency, so prefer External Functions when the external computation is expensive or unique per row. When testing, check error messages carefully—authorization errors usually indicate prefix or role problems, while runtime errors may come from the function logic. Final question to reflect on: how will you handle retries and timeouts for external calls in production queries?

keyIdea.title: Function mapping
keyIdea.text: An External Function declares a SQL-accessible name tied to a gateway endpoint and the API_INTEGRATION for secure invocation.

content.html:
Definition
CREATE EXTERNAL FUNCTION
Map a SQL callable function to your API endpoint and the API_INTEGRATION you created earlier.
-- As a role with CREATE EXTERNAL FUNCTION privilege
CREATE OR REPLACE EXTERNAL FUNCTION my_external_sentiment_analyzer(text VARCHAR)
  RETURNS VARCHAR
  API_INTEGRATION = my_api_integration
  AS 'https://abcdef123.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/prod/my_function';
Call it like any UDF: SELECT my_external_sentiment_analyzer('I love this product');
Snowflake serializes the input and deserializes the response for SQL use.
Ensure the AS URL matches an allowed prefix in your integration.
Pro Tip

Start by calling the function on a single test row and inspect returned values and error messages before scaling to many rows.

Example Scenario
You have a product reviews table and want a sentiment label for each row. Define an External Function that calls an existing sentiment API. Test on a small sample to measure latency and accuracy, then consider batched enrichment outside queries if cost is high.
Common mistake
Treating external calls as zero-latency operations. They are network calls with potential failures; design queries and error handling accordingly.
Key Takeaway

An External Function is a SQL facade over an external endpoint. Verify integration prefixes and role permissions, and plan for latency and retries.

screens.title: Stored Procedures: Purpose and Languages
screens.narratorSegment: Stored Procedures let you bundle multi-statement logic and control flow inside Snowflake. They can perform DDL and DML, run conditional logic, and orchestrate multiple steps that are awkward to express in a single S Q L statement. Snowflake supports multiple languages for procedures, including S Q L scripting and JavaScript; other languages like Python were mentioned as preview at times. S Q L scripting is native and useful for straightforward procedural tasks that stay in S Q L, while JavaScript is common for more complex control flow, variable handling, and error management. Choose JavaScript when you need robust procedural primitives like loops and in-memory logic, and select S Q L scripting when you prefer the simplicity and directness of S Q L commands. A common misconception is that Stored Procedures are only for administrative tasks — they are also useful for ETL orchestration and reusable business logic. Security considerations include the EXECUTE AS clause, which controls whether the procedure runs with the caller's privileges or the owner's privileges; use EXECUTE AS OWNER carefully to grant needed capabilities without exposing unnecessary rights. Example: use a stored procedure to create a table if it doesn’t exist, then perform updates and return a status message. What kind of daily automation in your workflows could you encapsulate in a procedure?

Definition
Stored Procedures in Snowflake
Encapsulate multi-step DDL/DML and control flow inside Snowflake using SQL scripting or JavaScript.
Use SQL scripting for native SQL procedural tasks and DDL constructs.
Use JavaScript when you need variables, loops, or complex control flow and result handling.
Security: choose EXECUTE AS OWNER or CALLER depending on privilege needs; OWNER can grant elevated power.
Why it matters

Stored Procedures let you automate recurring tasks and encapsulate business logic close to the data, reducing extract-transform-load work.

Language choice snapshot
SQL Scripting: native, good for DDL/DML and simple loops.
JavaScript: richer control flow, statement objects, and result handling.
Common misconception
Procedures are not only for DBAs. They are a tool for automation, ETL orchestration, and encapsulating business rules within Snowflake.
Key Takeaway

Pick the language that fits the control flow needs: SQL scripting for native statements, JavaScript for procedural richness.

screens.title: SQL Scripting Stored Procedure Example
screens.narratorSegment: Here is a simple S Q L scripting stored procedure that creates a table if it does not exist and returns a confirmation message. The key idea is EXECUTE IMMEDIATE, which runs dynamic S Q L built from input values. Unlike JavaScript procedures, S Q L scripting keeps the logic in S Q L and is easy to reason about for DDL or DML tasks. In practice, validate table names or identifiers to avoid injection-like problems. The example uses a bind-like placeholder style with the :table_name variable inside the script body. After creating the procedure, call it with CALL create_table_if_not_exists('my_new_table'); and then verify the table exists with a simple SELECT from the information schema or a DESCRIBE. A common mistake is constructing object names without validation. Also consider whether users who call the procedure need direct privileges to create objects; use EXECUTE AS OWNER if the procedure must run with the creator's privileges, but perform a security review. Takeaway: S Q L scripting procedures are concise for DDL orchestration, but validate inputs and document privileges before production deployment. SQL Scripting Stored Procedure Example means use execute immediate for dynamic ddl inside a sql stored procedure, and validate identifier inputs to avoid misuse.. In practical terms, create a table conditionally and return a status message. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: SQL scripting pattern
keyIdea.text: Use EXECUTE IMMEDIATE for dynamic DDL inside a SQL stored procedure, and validate identifier inputs to avoid misuse.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
SQL Stored Procedure
Creates a table if it does not exist and returns a message.
-- As a role with CREATE PROCEDURE privilege
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE create_table_if_not_exists(table_name VARCHAR)
RETURNS VARCHAR
LANGUAGE SQL
AS
$$
BEGIN
    EXECUTE IMMEDIATE 'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ' || :table_name || ' (id INT, name VARCHAR)';
    RETURN 'Table ' || :table_name || ' created or already exists.';
END;
$$;

CALL create_table_if_not_exists('my_new_table');
Verify by querying INFORMATION_SCHEMA or running a SELECT on the new table. Always sanitize or validate table_name to prevent unintended object creation.
Explanation and tips
  • EXECUTE IMMEDIATE runs the constructed SQL string at runtime.
  • SQL scripting procedures are ideal for administrative and DDL orchestration.
  • Consider privileges: does the caller need CREATE TABLE rights, or should the procedure use EXECUTE AS OWNER?
Common mistake
Concatenating unvalidated identifiers can create security or management problems. Validate names against a whitelist when possible.
Key Takeaway

SQL scripting procedures are compact for DDL tasks. Use EXECUTE IMMEDIATE responsibly and validate identifiers.

screens.title: JavaScript Stored Procedure Example
screens.narratorSegment: JavaScript stored procedures are a popular choice when you need procedural control, result inspection, or conditional logic combined with S Q L execution. The pattern uses snowflake. createStatement to run S Q L, then result_set. next and getColumnValue to read results. In the example, a procedure counts rows in a table, conditionally performs an update, and returns a message describing the action. Notice how variables are used to build the S Q L command and how statement. execute returns a result set that you iterate. Important safety tips: avoid building S Q L with unvalidated external input; prefer binds when the A P I supports them. Also, avoid row-by-row loops over large datasets inside JavaScript; where possible, express set-based operations in S Q L and call them from the procedure. A common misconception is that JavaScript procedures are suitable for heavy per-row processing; instead, use them to orchestrate set-based S Q L operations or small control-flow tasks. Example takeaway: use JavaScript to coordinate complex steps and read results, but push data-heavy work into S Q L statements executed by the procedure.

keyIdea.title: JS procedure pattern
keyIdea.text: Use snowflake.createStatement to run SQL and handle results; prefer set-based SQL inside procedures and bind parameters when possible.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
JavaScript Stored Procedure
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE process_customer_data(table_name VARCHAR)
RETURNS VARCHAR
LANGUAGE JAVASCRIPT
AS
$$
var sql_command = "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM " + TABLE_NAME;
var statement = snowflake.createStatement( {sqlText: sql_command} );
var result_set = statement.execute();
result_set.next();
var count = result_set.getColumnValue(1);

if (count > 0) {
    snowflake.execute({sqlText: "UPDATE " + TABLE_NAME + " SET name = UPPER(name)"});
    return "Processed " + count + " rows in " + TABLE_NAME + ". Names uppercased.";
} else {
    return "No data to process in " + TABLE_NAME + ".";
}
$$;

CALL process_customer_data('my_new_table');
Explanation
The procedure constructs and runs SQL, reads results, and conditionally executes further statements.
Use snowflake.createStatement to prepare a statement and execute to obtain a result set.
Avoid inefficient row-by-row loops; prefer single SQL UPDATE statements executed inside the procedure.
Security & performance notes
Validate input identifiers, consider EXECUTE AS settings for privileges, and keep data-heavy processing in set-based SQL for performance.
Key Takeaway

JavaScript procedures give procedural flexibility; use them to orchestrate SQL rather than to iterate large datasets inefficiently.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Create table and procedure
Set up a small table and a procedure that increases salaries by a percentage. Use binds to pass the percentage safely into the statement. 
CREATE TABLE employees (
  id INT,
  first_name VARCHAR,
  last_name VARCHAR,
  salary DECIMAL(10, 2)
);

INSERT INTO employees VALUES
(1, 'John', 'Doe', 60000.00),
(2, 'Jane', 'Smith', 75000.00),
(3, 'Peter', 'Jones', 50000.00);

CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE adjust_salaries(percentage_increase FLOAT)
RETURNS VARCHAR
LANGUAGE JAVASCRIPT
AS
$$
var current_date = new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10);
var sql_command = "UPDATE employees SET salary = salary * (1 + ?) WHERE salary < 100000";
var statement = snowflake.createStatement({
  sqlText: sql_command,
  binds: [PERCENTAGE_INCREASE]
});
var result = statement.execute();
var rows_affected = statement.getRowsAffected();
return "Salaries adjusted for " + rows_affected + " employees on " + current_date + ".";
$$;

CALL adjust_salaries(0.10);
Verification
Run SELECT * FROM employees; after each CALL to confirm salary changes. Use small datasets to test and measure behavior before applying to production tables.
Common Pitfall
Using string concatenation for numeric binds or identifiers can open up injection risks. Prefer binds for parameter values and validate object names separately.
Key Takeaway

Practice with small datasets, use binds for safety, and prefer set-based updates inside procedures for performance.

screens.title: Conceptual External Function Setup (Hands-on Outline)
screens.narratorSegment: Deploying a full External Function requires cloud resources, but you can perform the Snowflake-side steps conceptually and validate your S Q L and configuration. Start by identifying your cloud account ID and the gateway region. Create or confirm an IAM role that your A P I Gateway will use and that Snowflake can assume, then list the gateway URL prefixes you will authorize. Use the CREATE OR REPLACE A P I INTEGRATION statement with these values. Next, define the EXTERNAL FUNCTION using the gateway URL and the integration reference. Test by calling the function in a single-row SELECT to validate serialization and basic behavior. If you cannot deploy the cloud components, review the S Q L templates and confirm placeholders are accurate. Important security checks include verifying the role ARN, ensuring the allowed prefix matches the gateway stage properly, and confirming that the gateway enforces authentication or access control. A common misconception is that this S Q L will automatically provision cloud resources; it will not. The Snowflake S Q L only registers the integration and function metadata. Reflection: when you do provision cloud resources, who will own and audit the IAM role and gateway configuration in your organization?

Process Flow
Conceptual Setup Checklist
  1. Identify cloud account ID and gateway region.
  2. Prepare an IAM role for Snowflake to assume.
  3. Record API gateway URL prefixes for API_ALLOWED_PREFIXES.
  4. Create API INTEGRATION with provider, role ARN, and prefixes.
  5. Create EXTERNAL FUNCTION referencing the integration and endpoint.
  6. Run a single-row SELECT to test invocation and response.
Example SQL Templates
-- Conceptual: create integration and external function (placeholders must be replaced)
CREATE OR REPLACE API INTEGRATION my_sentiment_api_integration
  API_PROVIDER = AWS_API_GATEWAY
  API_AWS_ROLE_ARN = 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/snowflake_api_role'
  ENABLED = TRUE
  API_ALLOWED_PREFIXES = ('https://abcdef123.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/prod/sentiment');

CREATE OR REPLACE EXTERNAL FUNCTION get_sentiment(input_text VARCHAR)
  RETURNS VARCHAR
  API_INTEGRATION = my_sentiment_api_integration
  AS 'https://abcdef123.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/prod/sentiment';
If you can't provision cloud resources in this lab, review the placeholders and test the SQL syntax locally. Ensure your team controls the IAM role and gateway configuration when deployed.
Common mistake

Assuming Snowflake will create or configure cloud resources. Snowflake only stores integration metadata; cloud setup is separate.

screens.title: Choosing Between External Functions and Stored Procedures
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding whether to use an External Function or a Stored Procedure depends on your goals. External Functions are appropriate when you need to call an existing external service or specialized compute per row, such as a third-party A P I for enrichment or a machine learning model hosted as a serverless function. They integrate directly into S Q L but add network latency and depend on gateway and cloud permissions. Stored Procedures run entirely inside Snowflake, so they are ideal for orchestrating multiple S Q L statements, performing DDL/DML, and automating workflows without external network calls. Security-wise, External Functions rely on A P I Integration and cloud IAM; Stored Procedures rely on EXECUTE AS settings to control privilege elevation. Performance-wise, prefer Stored Procedures for set-based data transformations and External Functions for unique row-level enrichment where external logic cannot be replicated in S Q L. A common misconception is using an External Function where a single S Q L UPDATE inside a procedure would be faster and simpler. The practical question to ask: can the logic be expressed as set-based S Q L inside Snowflake, or does it require external compute? That question will guide the correct choice.

content.html:
Comparison
External Function vs Stored Procedure
External Function
Calls external serverless code, good for per-row enrichment, requires API Integration and gateway, adds network latency.
Stored Procedure
Runs inside Snowflake, performs DDL/DML orchestration, supports SQL scripting and JavaScript, ideal for automation.
Security: External Functions use cloud IAM and API Integration; Stored Procedures use EXECUTE AS OWNER/CALLER semantics.
Performance: prefer set-based SQL inside procedures; use External Functions only when external compute is necessary per row.
Scenario guidance
If you have an existing Lambda that performs a unique prediction per row, use an External Function. If you need to create tables, update many rows, and perform checks, encapsulate that logic in a Stored Procedure.
Misconception
Don't default to External Functions for heavy transformations. They are best for specialized, external-only operations.
Key Takeaway

Ask whether the work can be expressed in set-based SQL inside Snowflake. If not, an External Function may be appropriate.

screens.title: Security and Performance Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Security and performance considerations are central to safe use of External Functions and Stored Procedures. For External Functions, ensure API_AWS_ROLE_ARN and API_ALLOWED_PREFIXES are accurate, and validate that the A P I Gateway enforces access controls and input validation. For Stored Procedures, carefully choose EXECUTE AS OWNER or CALLER to balance privilege needs with least privilege principles. Avoid concatenating unvalidated inputs into S Q L strings; prefer binds and validate identifiers on a whitelist when necessary. For performance, keep heavy transformations set-based and execute them as a single S Q L statement inside a procedure, rather than iterating rows in JavaScript. When using External Functions, test at scale to measure network latency and the cloud function's cold-start behavior, and design retries and timeouts appropriately in your calling logic. Log and monitor procedure calls and external invocations to support auditing and troubleshooting. A common misconception is that using EXECUTE AS OWNER removes the need for auditing; you still must track who invoked the procedure. Final reflective question: what combination of logging, input validation, and privilege configuration will your team adopt to keep these extensions safe in production?

Best Practices
Security Checklist
  • Verify API_ALLOWED_PREFIXES and role ARNs before testing.
  • Ensure the gateway enforces auth and input validation.
  • Use EXECUTE AS OWNER only after security review and logging.
  • Prefer binds and validate identifiers against whitelists.
Performance & Operational Guidance
Keep data-heavy work in SQL, avoid per-row JavaScript loops for large datasets.
Measure latency for External Functions and plan retries/timeouts.
Instrument and log procedure and external calls for audit and debugging.
Key Takeaway

Combine input validation, least privilege execution, and monitoring to safely use External Functions and Stored Procedures in production.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: A few final concepts to remember about stored procedures and procedural security. A Stored Procedure is a block of code executed inside Snowflake and can be written in S Q L scripting or JavaScript; it can perform DDL and DML and return messages or results. S Q L scripting is native and best for straightforward DDL orchestration, while JavaScript provides greater procedural control through statement objects and result inspection. The EXECUTE AS clause determines whether the procedure runs as the caller or as the owner; EXECUTE AS OWNER can grant broader privileges but must be used with caution and auditing. Finally, serverless functions host the external code for External Functions, and you should design for retries, timeouts, and error handling. Keep these distinctions in mind when you decide how to encapsulate logic and who should own the privileges for execution.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will explore two complementary extension points in Snowflake: External Functions and Stored Procedures. External Functions let your S Q L queries call out to existing serverless services, enabling row-level enrichment, validation, or specialized compute that lives outside Snowflake. Stored Procedures let you encapsulate multi-step logic, DDL and DML, and control flow inside Snowflake using S Q L scripting or JavaScript. You'll learn the architecture for an External Function — how an A P I Integration and an A P I Gateway route a request to a serverless function — and the key S Q L commands used to register that integration and the function itself. You will also see Stored Procedure examples that show how to create tables conditionally, run queries from JavaScript, bind parameters, and handle results. I will point out common mistakes, like misconfigured allowed prefixes or concatenating unvalidated input into S Q L strings, and practical trade-offs, such as network latency for external calls versus the power of in-platform execution. By the end you'll know when to choose an External Function and when a Stored Procedure is the right tool, and you'll have concrete examples to try in a live coding demo.

By the end of this chapter you will have four practical skills. First, you will understand the architecture and typical use cases for External Functions, which lets you call secure serverless endpoints from S Q L. I will explain why that matters with a concrete example: enriching rows with a sentiment call to an existing model. Second, you will be able to configure an A P I Integration and register an External Function in Snowflake. You will see the key S Q L commands and the security placeholders that must be correct to avoid authorization errors. Third, you will be able to explain the purpose and benefits of Stored Procedures, including when to use S Q L scripting versus JavaScript for procedural logic. Finally, you will write and execute a basic JavaScript stored procedure, use binds for safety, and inspect results. Each objective includes a short mnemonic or visual to help you remember the steps and a verified competency milestone so you can self-assess when you're ready to move on.

This second objectives slide describes the hands-on skills you will practice. You'll create a small employees table and then write a JavaScript stored procedure to update salaries, which teaches binding parameters and reading results from a statement. Then you will conceptually set up an A P I Integration and an External Function using the S Q L patterns shown; even though deploying a real serverless function is outside this activity, knowing the placeholders and security checks is essential. You'll also review common mistakes like misconfigured allowed prefixes or role ARNs and test edge cases that surface network latency or permission failures. Each objective pairs a short procedural checklist and a verification step so you can mark progress: create table, insert test rows, write and call the procedure, and run conceptual DDL for A P I Integration. These exercises reinforce both the syntax and the operational considerations you need to apply these features safely in production.

External Functions let Snowflake queries call code that runs outside the platform. The architecture centers on three pieces: an A P I Integration object in Snowflake, an A P I Gateway that acts as a front door, and a serverless function that executes your logic. The A P I Integration stores the trust relationship and allowed endpoint prefixes; the gateway routes the request to the serverless function; and Snowflake serializes inputs and deserializes outputs for S Q L consumption. A typical use case is enriching rows with third-party data — for example, calling a sentiment model for each row of text. This is powerful because it avoids extract-transform-load cycles, but it introduces network latency, so it is best for cases where the external logic is complex and cannot be efficiently implemented in S Q L. Common misconfigurations include incorrect allowed prefixes and role ARNs, which lead to authorization failures. As a concrete example, imagine calling a sentiment endpoint for each product review during a reporting query; use sampling in testing and measure latency. A misconception to avoid is thinking External Functions are free of operational cost: they rely on your cloud functions and gateway, so plan for retries, throttling, and error handling. Takeaway: use External Functions when external compute is essential and row-level enrichment value outweighs network cost. How would you measure whether the network cost is acceptable for your query pattern?

Creating an A P I Integration is the first concrete step to enable External Functions. This process establishes a trust relationship and records which endpoints Snowflake may call. The S Q L pattern starts with CREATE OR REPLACE A P I INTEGRATION, followed by provider-specific parameters and API_ALLOWED_PREFIXES that list the gateway URL prefixes. For AWS A P I Gateway you provide an IAM role ARN which Snowflake will assume; for other providers similar values are required. A common error is forgetting to include the full URL prefix in API_ALLOWED_PREFIXES; this will cause authorization failures when the External Function is invoked. As an example, imagine you have an A P I Gateway URL that ends with a path to your function. Include the prefix up to the function base path in API_ALLOWED_PREFIXES. Always test the integration with a minimal external function call and check the error messages — they usually indicate whether the failure is due to the role ARN or allowed prefixes. Misconception: the A P I Integration does not deploy your function; it only authorizes Snowflake to call a gateway. After the integration, you still need to define the External Function that references the gateway endpoint. Try a dry run with one test row to validate the configuration before bulk use.

Once the A P I Integration is in place, define an External Function that references the gateway endpoint. The CREATE OR REPLACE EXTERNAL FUNCTION statement maps a function name and parameter signature to a URL. Snowflake treats the function like any other UDF in S Q L, so you can SELECT it or use it in transformations. The important security detail is that the function uses API_INTEGRATION to assert the trust established earlier, and the endpoint must match the allowed prefix. An example call looks like SELECT my_external_sentiment_analyzer('This product is great!'); which returns a VARCHAR result from the external service. A misconception to clear up: defining the External Function does not automatically make the external service secure; you must ensure the gateway and function enforce appropriate authorization and input validation. Also, external calls introduce per-row network latency, so prefer External Functions when the external computation is expensive or unique per row. When testing, check error messages carefully—authorization errors usually indicate prefix or role problems, while runtime errors may come from the function logic. Final question to reflect on: how will you handle retries and timeouts for external calls in production queries?

Stored Procedures let you bundle multi-statement logic and control flow inside Snowflake. They can perform DDL and DML, run conditional logic, and orchestrate multiple steps that are awkward to express in a single S Q L statement. Snowflake supports multiple languages for procedures, including S Q L scripting and JavaScript; other languages like Python were mentioned as preview at times. S Q L scripting is native and useful for straightforward procedural tasks that stay in S Q L, while JavaScript is common for more complex control flow, variable handling, and error management. Choose JavaScript when you need robust procedural primitives like loops and in-memory logic, and select S Q L scripting when you prefer the simplicity and directness of S Q L commands. A common misconception is that Stored Procedures are only for administrative tasks — they are also useful for ETL orchestration and reusable business logic. Security considerations include the EXECUTE AS clause, which controls whether the procedure runs with the caller's privileges or the owner's privileges; use EXECUTE AS OWNER carefully to grant needed capabilities without exposing unnecessary rights. Example: use a stored procedure to create a table if it doesn’t exist, then perform updates and return a status message. What kind of daily automation in your workflows could you encapsulate in a procedure?

Here is a simple S Q L scripting stored procedure that creates a table if it does not exist and returns a confirmation message. The key idea is EXECUTE IMMEDIATE, which runs dynamic S Q L built from input values. Unlike JavaScript procedures, S Q L scripting keeps the logic in S Q L and is easy to reason about for DDL or DML tasks. In practice, validate table names or identifiers to avoid injection-like problems. The example uses a bind-like placeholder style with the :table_name variable inside the script body. After creating the procedure, call it with CALL create_table_if_not_exists('my_new_table'); and then verify the table exists with a simple SELECT from the information schema or a DESCRIBE. A common mistake is constructing object names without validation. Also consider whether users who call the procedure need direct privileges to create objects; use EXECUTE AS OWNER if the procedure must run with the creator's privileges, but perform a security review. Takeaway: S Q L scripting procedures are concise for DDL orchestration, but validate inputs and document privileges before production deployment. SQL Scripting Stored Procedure Example means use execute immediate for dynamic ddl inside a sql stored procedure, and validate identifier inputs to avoid misuse.. In practical terms, create a table conditionally and return a status message. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

JavaScript stored procedures are a popular choice when you need procedural control, result inspection, or conditional logic combined with S Q L execution. The pattern uses snowflake. createStatement to run S Q L, then result_set. next and getColumnValue to read results. In the example, a procedure counts rows in a table, conditionally performs an update, and returns a message describing the action. Notice how variables are used to build the S Q L command and how statement. execute returns a result set that you iterate. Important safety tips: avoid building S Q L with unvalidated external input; prefer binds when the A P I supports them. Also, avoid row-by-row loops over large datasets inside JavaScript; where possible, express set-based operations in S Q L and call them from the procedure. A common misconception is that JavaScript procedures are suitable for heavy per-row processing; instead, use them to orchestrate set-based S Q L operations or small control-flow tasks. Example takeaway: use JavaScript to coordinate complex steps and read results, but push data-heavy work into S Q L statements executed by the procedure.

Deciding whether to use an External Function or a Stored Procedure depends on your goals. External Functions are appropriate when you need to call an existing external service or specialized compute per row, such as a third-party A P I for enrichment or a machine learning model hosted as a serverless function. Stored Procedures run entirely inside Snowflake, so they are ideal for orchestrating multiple S Q L statements, performing DDL/DML, and automating workflows without external network calls. A few final concepts to remember about stored procedures and procedural security. A Stored Procedure is a block of code executed inside Snowflake and can be written in S Q L scripting or JavaScript; it can perform DDL and DML and return messages or results. S Q L scripting is native and best for straightforward DDL orchestration, while JavaScript provides greater procedural control through statement objects and result inspection.
